24. As per section 118 and 139 of N.I.Act initial presumption is on the respondent to prove that he had paid the amount, not returned the said amount then issued the cheque, same was presented for encashment, cheque was returned for insufficient funds.

Thereafter he ought to issue the notice,
then the said presumption is to be rebutted by the appellant by producing the evidence and documents.

But in this case from the evidence of RW1 he has not made out that he is not running chit business and respondent has not invested in the said chit and he is liable to pay an amount of Rs.7,48,000/- and not issued the Ex.P1 for discharge of debt.
Therefore by considering the entire evidence and documents respondent has proved his case by producing the documents and evidence.
There is no reason to interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
Appellate court may interfere in the judgment of trial court when trial court has not considered the provisions of law nor evidence placed by the parties.
Under such circumstances the appellate court may interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
In the present case no such fault found in the judgment passed by the trial court.

25. In the case of (2010 AIR SCO296 Rangappa Vs Mohan wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the presumption that the cheque was drawn in discharge of legally recoverable debt is a presumption of law that ought to be raised in every case.

Accused has failed to produce the presumption available under section 118 and 139 of N.I. act.
26.

However based on the above said judgments the accused has not produced the rebuttal evidence, the accused has not proved his defence.
Therefore there is no need to interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
Accordingly, Point No.1 is answered in the Negative.

K Shridhar vs Y S Santosh on 14 August, 2024
Kabc010224982021
 In The Court Of The Lxii Addl.City Civil &
 Sessions Judge (Cch-63), Bengaluru.
Dated: This The 14 th Day Of August, 2024
 Present
Sri A. Earanna, M.Com., Ll.M.,
 Lxii Addl. City Civil & Sessions Judge,
 Bengaluru.
Criminal Appeal No. 744/2021
Appellant/ Sri. K. Shridhar
Accused : S/o Late Krishnappa
 Aged about 40 years
 R/at No.20, Aditya Nagar,
 Kothnuru
 Bengaluru South
 Bengaluru-560 078
(By Shireen Taj, Advocate)
 Vs
Respondent/ Sri. Y.S. Santosh
Complainant: Aged about 46 years
 S/o Y. R. Seetharama Rao
 R/at No.47, 4th Cross,
 23rd main, Manjunatha colony
 J.P. Nagar
 Bengaluru-560 078
 (By K.S.V, Advocate)
 Judgment
This is a criminal appeal preferred by the appellant/accused under Section 374(3) of Cr.P.C., being aggrieved by the conviction judgment passed by the learned XVI Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bengaluru, dated 28.09.2021 in C.C.No. 24750/2017.
17. At this juncture, this Court relied the following Judgments:
AIR 1992 Supreme Court 1604 Jagadish Singh-Appellant -Vs- Natthu Singh- Respondent:
(A) General Clauses Act, S.27-Notice - Presumption of service - Refusal by addressee to accept - Notice must be presumed to have been served.
opennyai_summary.facts:
The appellant is the accused and respondent is the complainant before the Trial Court.
The complainant further contends that, some of the chit schemes in which he had invested earlier ie from the year 2009 had given him good returns, in view of which he was attracted to invest in further schemes that were floated by the accused, and had made his bid for a chit scheme and was liable to be paid an amount of Rs.7,48,000/- but quite unfortunately, even after the bidding process had been concluded, the accused did not pay the promised money to him, for which he pestered the accused on several occasions for payment disbursement, whereas the accused had been dodging the issue by stating that, he would pay the same within a short period of time, he being eager about his payment, was also quite confident in receiving the same, as the past conduct of the accused stood testimonial to his behavior then.
Hence he has filed this present complainant against the Accused for the offence punishable U/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
The Trial Court erred in law in accepting and acting upon the evidence of P.W.1 which is being inadmissible.
After considering the entire evidence and documents the court has rightly passed the judgment.
After passing the judgment appellant ought to pay the amount.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
The accused contended that the Judgment of the Trial Court is perverse,
illegal and un-sustainable under law.
Respondent was a member of the chits.
Instead of payment of the said amount he had issued the cheque same was presented for encashment, cheque was dishonored as funds insufficient.
opennyai_summary.issue:
10. The following points arise for the consideration of the court :-
1) Whether the appellant has made out grounds to allow the appeal ?
2) What order?
11.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
No doubt that before filing the complaint U/s 138 of N.I. Act complainant ought to issue the notice.
As per Section 27 of General Clause Act, if the notice was issued to the correct address, then the notice was returned as not claimed, returned to sender, then as per the above said section notice was deemed served.
Evidence Act (1 of 1872),
S.114.
(1996) 7 Supreme Court cases 523: State of MP Vs Hiralal and Others (A) Supreme Court Rules, 1966 -Pt.II, Or.XV, R.11 - Notice to respondent - Service of - Addressee respondents managing to have the notices returned with postal remarks "not available in the house", "house locked" and "shop closed" respectively - Held, notices must be deemed to have been served on the respondents - Evidence Act, 1872, S. 114,
III. (e) - General Clauses Act, 1897, S.27.
18.
From the evidence of PW1 it has not brought that he was having license to run travel agency.
Under such circumstances mere non production of the document, court cannot come to conclusion that he was not having sources of income.
No doubt respondent has not produced any document to come to conclusion he had paid the said amount.
If he has not running the chit fund then he may produce the document before the court stating that respondent has not member of the said chit and he has not paid the chit amount.
When the appellant has taken defence he has issued the Ex.P1 for discharge of debt, then in this regard he has got golden opportunity to prove his defence by producing the document.
Mere non production of the document by the respondent it cannot come to conclusion that respondent is not having income or sources of income to pay the chit amount.
More over he has taken defence that he had paid three cheques to one Ravikumar.
Out of which one cheque had paid to the complainant by the Ravikumar, said cheque was mis used by the complainant.
Therefore considering all the aspects there is no grounds to interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
24. As per section 118 and 139 of N.I.Act initial presumption is on the respondent to prove that he had paid the amount, not returned the said amount then issued the cheque, same was presented for encashment, cheque was returned for insufficient funds.
Thereafter he ought to issue the notice,
then the said presumption is to be rebutted by the appellant by producing the evidence and documents.
But in this case from the evidence of RW1 he has not made out that he is not running chit business and respondent has not invested in the said chit and he is liable to pay an amount of Rs.7,48,000/- and not issued the Ex.P1 for discharge of debt.
Therefore by considering the entire evidence and documents respondent has proved his case by producing the documents and evidence.
There is no reason to interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
Appellate court may interfere in the judgment of trial court when trial court has not considered the provisions of law nor evidence placed by the parties.
Under such circumstances the appellate court may interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
In the present case no such fault found in the judgment passed by the trial court.
25. In the case of (2010 AIR SCO296 Rangappa Vs Mohan wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the presumption that the cheque was drawn in discharge of legally recoverable debt is a presumption of law that ought to be raised in every case.
Accused has failed to produce the presumption available under section 118 and 139 of N.I. act.
26.
In addition to this in the case of T.P. Murugan (Dead) Through legal representatives Vs Bojan (2018 (8) SCC 469), the Hon'ble Cout has held that "once the cheque has been signed and issued in favour of the holder of the cheque, there is statutory presumption that the cheque is issued in respect of legally enforceable debt or liability".
In the present case the appellant has not denied the issuance of cheque and signature on the said cheque.
When the accused admitted the issuance of the cheque then burden lies on the appellant to prove that he has not issued cheque for discharge of debt or liability.
Therefore there is no need to interfere in the judgment passed by the trial court.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Accordingly, Point No.1 is answered in the Negative.
